references.text: The entire account of the blind man at Jericho is found in [ref:Luk 18:35-43|Luke 18:35-43]. Parallel accounts are found in [ref:Matt 20:29-34|Matthew 20:29-34] and [ref:Mark 10:46-52|Mark 10:46-52].

Mark's parallel account of the blind Bartimaeus at Jericho ([ref:Mark 10:46-52|Mark 10:46-52]). Mark names the blind man as Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, and places the event when Jesus was leaving Jericho.
Matthew's parallel account ([ref:Matt 20:29-34|Matthew 20:29-34]) mentions two blind men at Jericho who cried out to Jesus for healing.
Another account in [ref:Matt 9:27-31|Matthew 9:27-31] where two blind men follow Jesus and cry, "Have mercy on us, Son of David!", similar to the blind man's cry in Luke 18.
[ref:Luk 19:1|Luke 19:1] continues the account with Jesus entering Jericho and passing through the town, connecting to his approach to Jericho in this verse.
Jericho is also mentioned in the parable of the good Samaritan ([ref:Luk 10:30|Luke 10:30]), where the road from Jerusalem to Jericho serves as the setting for the events.

Jericho is a city with a long history in the Bible. In [ref:Jos 6:26|Joshua 6:26], Joshua pronounces a curse on anyone who rebuilds Jericho, highlighting the city's significance in the biblical narrative.
In [ref:Luk 7:21-22|Luke 7:21-22], Jesus heals many blind people and sends word to John that the blind see – a fulfillment of the messianic prophecy in Isaiah 35:5 and 61:1.
The prophecy in [ref:Jes 35:5|Isaiah 35:5] that the eyes of the blind will be opened in the messianic age. The healing of the blind man at Jericho is a fulfillment of this prophecy.
In [ref:Jes 42:7|Isaiah 42:7], it is prophesied about the Lord's servant who will open the eyes of the blind – a messianic prophecy pointing forward to Jesus' healings of the blind.
